newsitem.title: UK: Lehman sees Airbus pre-float sales surge.
newsitem.headline: Lehman sees Airbus pre-float sales surge.

text.p: Airbus Industrie, whose four European consortium members are working to merge their interests into one company by 1999, should grow swiftly in coming years and hit capital markets as a $10 billion firm, investment bank Lehman Brothers said in major research document.

The Lehman research, based entirely on estimated historical and prospective financial data, forecast a significant upturn in Airbus sales and profits over the next few years after which its business base should stabilise.
As an illustration of what this could mean, the report said the firm might potentially be worth as much as $15 to $18 billion.
Airbus is currently made up of four partners who are also subcontractors on its products.
France's Aerospatiale and German Daimler-Benz Aerospace have the largest stakes at 37.9 percent each, while British Aerospace Plc has 20 percent and Spain's CASA has 4.2 percent.
Lehman said an expected upturn across the commercial jet transport market "will raise its annual sales from just under $10 billion in 1995 to something just under $20 billion".
Thus Airbus will push forward sales and deliveries, and gain a base for a serious challenge on its long-standing strategic aim -- to achieve parity with industry leader Boeing Corp.
However, Lehman said that, although it saw good prospects for a new Airbus, it also saw a number of critical pressures.

"Airbus, reorganised into a single corporate entity (SCE), will find itself at an important crossroad in its corporate life. We believe that Airbus SCE represents an extraordinary and unrecognised company, and if its securities were to become available, they could represent an investment opportunity of significance and great value," Lehman wrote.
It said a decision to launch an entire programme, like the proposed 500-600 seat A3XX, would mean exceeding its internal cash flow resources and require it to sell equity or issue debt.

Although it felt obliged to make a very wide range of estimates for the next eight years, Lehman concluded that Airbus would need an injection of cash of at least $4.0 billion to complete the A3XX before deliveries started in 2003.

Given that the goals of creating a new entity and preparing the all-important new aircraft programme were so closely-related, Lehman predicted that Airbus "must, and therefore will, surprise observers with progress on the reorganisation front sooner rather than later."
It guessed that Airbus might aim to establish the new company by the time of the 1997 Paris Air Show.
